meta.notes: Layer 4: peak pricing (multiplier x elasticity on the campus_rush peak windows), SLA target x compensation, starvation cap at high load (campus_rush classes and peak profile with the network layer removed, three cross-trained clerks), and a combined good-manager scenario compared with the shipped baseline under common random numbers.
caveats: profit_per_hour subtracts the waiting cost of the served customers only, so demand shedding (higher price, fewer arrivals) looks profitable twice: fewer lost sales and less waiting cost. The profit-maximising multiplier therefore sits at the edge of the tested range and must not be read as a policy recommendation on its own.
Compensation is a pure transfer: it never changes service times, so los_p95 is identical across the SLA grid. Only capacity/pricing changes attainment.

campus_rush has no inventory layer (its scenario file carries no BOM), so the good-manager scenario covers pricing + SLA + fairness + network. Cross-layer inventory coupling is out of scope for this study.

The fairness experiment keeps campus_rush's demand profile, classes and patience, but drops the network layer and sets workers=3 so the queue is visible to the starvation cap; that is the split+fast high-load cell.
